name: Campaign Bible: Master of the Black Tower

pages.name: The Premise
pages.html:
Levels 1–20. Begins 18 Darkember 350 AC in Vogler. Ends in the Abyss, with a decision that is not yours to make.

The War of the Lance has begun, but western Ansalon has not yet felt it. That is the whole shape of Arc I: the characters travel across a continent during the last months in which travelling across it is merely difficult.

In the east it has already happened. Silvanesti is gone — not conquered, transformed, folded into Lorac's nightmare and left there. The expedition that went in to stop it did not come out.

What Changed

Caramon Majere is dead. He died inside the Silvanesti catastrophe in late 349 AC, along with every companion who went with him. Raistlin came out alone.

That single fact drives all twenty levels. Everything Raistlin does in this campaign — taking the Black, taking Wayreth, taking Palanthas, opening the Portal, binding the Abyss — proceeds from a man who has decided that his brother's death is a problem awaiting the correct spell.

He has not grieved. He has been working.

Three Facts to Establish Early

  1. Raistlin is Master of Wayreth, and has been for only a few months. He is not accepted. He is not trusted. The Tower does not care.
  2. The Tower chose him. Not the Conclave. This is public knowledge and nobody knows what to do with it.
  3. Nobody outside the Tower knows why he wants Palanthas. Including, for a long time, the party.

DM Note — The One-Sentence Version

A grieving man acquires the power to make sure nothing he loves can ever leave him again, and the campaign ends at the moment he finally has enough of it.

Everything else — the war, the Orders, the Portal, Takhisis — is context for that. When you are unsure how Raistlin would respond to something, ask whether it brings Caramon closer.

pages.name: Why Wayreth Chose Raistlin
pages.html:
Wayreth is not sentient the way a person is. It is closer to an old survival intelligence — centuries of enchantment, accumulated memory, the Forest, the Orders, and the wills of generations of archmages, settled into something that notices and prefers.

Silvanesti frightened it.

A Tower of High Sorcery watched another great repository of magic help destroy an entire nation. The Dragonarmies were rising. Dragons had returned. The gods were returning. And the Conclave was debating precedent.

What the Tower Did

It examined futures. Most ended badly — the Dragonarmies find Wayreth, the Orders fracture, the Towers fall, High Sorcery diminishes into hedge-magic and rumour.

In the small number where the Orders survived, one wizard kept appearing.

The Tower did not conclude that Raistlin Majere was good. It concluded that he was adaptable, ruthless, brilliant, inventive, impossible to intimidate, willing to use forbidden solutions, and extraordinarily difficult to kill.

Wayreth chose survival. Raistlin was the wizard most likely to provide it.

Survival and righteousness are not the same thing.

The Tower can determine what preserves High Sorcery. It cannot determine whether the price is acceptable. That judgement falls to the characters, and the campaign will eventually ask them for it directly.

DM Note — Do Not Make the Tower a Villain

The temptation is to reveal late that Wayreth was manipulating everyone. Resist it. The Tower is doing exactly what it says: choosing whatever survives. It has no capacity for morality and no pretence of any, and that is far more unsettling than malice.

The horror is not that the Tower is evil. It is that the Tower is correct, and correct is not enough.

pages.name: The Garden Incident
pages.html:
Mid-350 AC. The morning the Tower changed hands without anyone deciding it should.

Par-Salian took his customary walk through the gardens surrounding Wayreth.

When he tried to return, the path did not lead back. He tried another; it returned him to the same fountain. Another put him beneath the same silver-leaved tree. He attempted magical transportation and the spell set him down at the garden gate.

The Tower was visible through the trees. He simply could not reach it.

Inside, doors that had answered to him for thirty years stopped recognising his authority. Staircases shifted. Passages closed. Wards rewrote themselves. The Master's chambers sealed.

At Almost the Same Hour

Raistlin arrived at the Forest.

The Forest opened. The road appeared. The gates unlocked before he touched them. Staircases rearranged themselves around his movements. Magical lights that had not burned in centuries woke as he passed. The doors to the Master's chambers opened.

The great bells of Wayreth rang without being touched.

The central wards recorded him not as guest, not as initiate, not as Black Robe, not as a member of the Conclave. They recorded him as Master.

Afterward

Par-Salian remained in the gardens until sunset. When the Tower finally let him back in, Raistlin was sitting in the Master's chamber.

The Conclave held a vote. The vote did not appoint Raistlin — it acknowledged what Wayreth had already done. Par-Salian called for it himself, rather than let the Orders fracture over whether to obey their own Tower.

DM Note — Playing Par-Salian

He was not deposed by an enemy. He was declined by a building he had served his whole life, and then he stood up in front of twenty-one people and asked them to ratify it.

He believes he did the right thing. He cannot stop testing that belief, and he tests it on the party — asking their opinion of decisions they have no context for, which is the tell.

He is the party's most likely patron, and he is not a dishonest man. He simply asks for help without explaining what the help is for.

pages.name: Raistlin's Descent: The Seven Stages
pages.html:
He does not begin wanting godhood. He arrives at it one reasonable step at a time, and every step is the obvious consequence of the one before.

Track where he is. The party should be able to feel the ground moving without being told.

StageThe reasoningSurfaces in
OneSilvanesti proved catastrophic magic can trap, damage or displace souls. Caramon died inside such a catastrophe. Conventional resurrection cannot reach him.Arc I — background
TwoFistandantilus studied recovering souls beyond normal resurrection. Therefore Fistandantilus may have found something that reaches Caramon.Arc II
ThreeFistandantilus's lost work is connected to Palanthas. Therefore Raistlin needs the cursed Tower.Arc II
FourThe Palanthas Tower holds a Portal into the Abyss. Therefore Caramon may be reachable from beyond the world's ordinary boundaries.Arc III
FiveThe Portal can summon and bind creatures of the Abyss. Therefore those creatures can be turned against Takhisis.Arc V
SixFistandantilus's work suggests death can be manipulated through memory, soul anchors, time and domination. Therefore death may not be a law at all.Arc IV
SevenIf death can be controlled, war can be controlled. If demons can be controlled, the Abyss can. If souls can be controlled, loss can. And if loss can be controlled, he never has to survive Caramon again.Arc VI

Where Love Becomes Possession

Between Six and Seven. Everything up to Six is a man trying to get his brother back. Seven is a man deciding that nothing he loves will ever be permitted to leave.

The party will not notice the transition when it happens. They will notice about two sessions later, and the delay is the point.

Running Him

  • He never argues from emotion. Every position is presented as the only reasonable conclusion, and it usually is.
  • He does not lie to the party. He omits, at enormous scale.
  • He does not mention Caramon. Not once, voluntarily, before Arc III. When the party raises it, he changes the subject with visible effort.
  • Caramon's sword hangs above the hearth in his chamber. Nobody touches it. He never explains it.

pages.name: Themes and the Central Question
pages.html:
Grief Versus Possession

Loving someone does not entitle you to keep them. The whole campaign is a twenty-level argument about that sentence.

Law Versus Compassion

The White Robes' failure was never that they had rules. It was treating obedience to those rules as inherently moral. Par-Salian confiscated research that might have saved a man, correctly, by the law, and the consequence was the Black Robe now sitting in his chair.

Survival Versus Goodness

Wayreth chose Raistlin because he preserves High Sorcery. That does not license everything he does to accomplish it.

Power and Consent

Necromancy, resurrection, demon-binding, and eventually Raistlin's entire philosophy all turn on one question: may another being be controlled for a supposedly greater purpose? The campaign asks it about demons, then about the war dead, then about Caramon, then about everyone.

History Repeating

Raistlin fears becoming Fistandantilus. He also fears becoming Par-Salian. He does not appear to have considered a third option, and the White Robe PC is the person positioned to demonstrate one.

The Central Question

If I become powerful enough, nothing I love can ever be taken from me again.

— Raistlin, and he is not wrong

The campaign ends when he finally has enough power to make that statement true. The characters then decide whether a world in which nothing can escape Raistlin Majere is salvation, tyranny, or both.

Do not resolve this for them. There are five endings and none of them is marked correct.

pages.name: The White Robe PC
pages.html:
One player character should be a White Robe candidate. The campaign works without it and is substantially better with it.

They are the ideological counterweight. Raistlin does not hate them — he watches them, and he tests them, because he wants to know whether White inevitably becomes rigid, self-righteous, and incapable of a difficult compassionate choice.

He is asking whether Par-Salian was inevitable.

Why the Timing Matters

The Night of the Eye falls only months after Raistlin's own break with the White Robes and the confiscation of his research. A new White Robe taking the Test in his Tower, under his personal observation, weeks after he abandoned that Order in grief and fury, is not a coincidence the Tower arranged by accident.

Session Zero Framing

Tell the player three things and no more:

  • They have been summoned to Wayreth to take the Test of High Sorcery.
  • The Master of Wayreth is a Black Robe, which is unprecedented.
  • Their Order is not happy about either fact.

Do not tell them Raistlin will personally observe. Do not tell them what the Test contains.

DM Note — The Long Game

Raistlin wants the White Robe to prove him wrong. He does not know that yet, and will deny it if asked directly through most of the campaign.

The White Robe Bond tracker is the single most important number in the finale. At high Bond, Raistlin listens to that character in the Abyss when he will listen to nobody else — including Fistandantilus, including Takhisis, including Caramon.

If your table has no White Robe, transfer the role to whichever character most consistently argues with him rather than around him. Raistlin has no use for agreement.
